title: Separated by our deeds
hook: separated by our own deeds, we ask the Lord in mercy to unite us (Barah Maha, ang 133)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Barah Maha: twelve months, each with its own color of longing. Before Guru Arjan names a single month, he opens with a stanza about the separation itself.

Two old friends stop talking. Nobody can quite remember when. There wasn't a big fight. Just a missed call, a canceled plan, a comment taken the wrong way, a year of not reaching out. Each small choice made sense at the time. Then one day you realize there's a distance between you that you built yourselves, one brick at a time. Guru Arjan's Barah Maha begins exactly there: not with a month, but with how the distance got there, and who can close it.
screen: `TWO FRIENDS STOP TALKING.` → `NO BIG FIGHT, JUST SMALL CHOICES.` → `A DISTANCE WE BUILT OURSELVES.`

segments.voice: The opening stanza, on ang 133, in paraphrase: we are separated by the deeds we have done. Have mercy, Lord, and unite us with yourself. Kirat karam ke veechhurhe. Kirat is what has been done; karam is action; veechhurhe, the separated ones, torn apart. The stanza is honest about how it happened. Nobody else did it to us; our own doings built the distance. Yet the very next breath isn't despair. It's a request: kar kirpaa, have mercy. Unite us. Then Guru Arjan paints the tiredness: wandering in the four corners and the ten directions, we've grown weary and come to your sanctuary. And he reaches for two farm pictures every Punjabi listener would know. A cow that gives no milk is of no use. A crop without water withers and won't fetch a price. Life without the One, he's saying, is like that: dry, unproductive, missing its whole point. Without meeting the beloved Friend, where can anyone find rest? The homes and towns where the Beloved isn't present are like burning furnaces. Each month to come will have its own color, but the root is here: separation by our own deeds, and a longing only grace can meet. Notice the balance. The stanza doesn't excuse us; the distance is ours. But it doesn't ask us to close it alone, either. In Sikh teaching, both are true at once: we're responsible for our deeds, and reunion comes by the One's grace.
screen: `KIRAT KARAM: WHAT WE HAVE DONE.` · `HAVE MERCY, UNITE US.` · `A COW WITHOUT MILK, A CROP WITHOUT WATER.` · `OUR DEEDS, AND THE ONE'S GRACE.` · then, large: `UNITE US.`

segments.voice: Think of one distance in your life you helped build, with a person, with a part of yourself or, if this is your language, with God, and without arguing whose fault it was, just admit your bricks. Then let the opposite feeling come: a wish to close it. If you pray, hold the stanza's own request, kar kirpaa, have mercy; if you don't, simply hold the wish.
Veechhurhe, the separated ones, torn apart: the opening of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha says we are veechhurhe by what we've done, and ask the One in mercy to unite us.
Your line: unite us. It's a humble request, not a verdict. See you in the month of Chet.

howItsDone: Sikhs read the opening stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha before the months, and its plea for reunion is heard whenever the Barah Maha is sung or read on sangrand.

chat.says: If we drifted from God by our own choices, isn't it on us alone to fix it?
options: Guru Arjan owns the distance as ours, but asks for mercy: reunion comes by the One's grace.
Guru Arjan says the distance isn't really our fault, so there's nothing to own or mend.
Guru Arjan says the distance closes by itself with time, so there's nothing to ask for.
chat.meaning: The opening stanza says we're separated by our own deeds, then asks, kar kirpaa: have mercy and unite us. Responsibility and grace together.
